{
  "ssotVersion": "1.9.2",
  "name": "acos-spec-engine",
  "description": "Native ACOS specification engine: structured, dependency-free spec-driven development lifecycle.",
  "lifecycle": {
    "constitution": {
      "id": "constitution",
      "name": "Constitution",
      "description": "Establish project principles, constraints, and authority boundaries before writing specifications.",
      "artifact": "constitution.md",
      "entrypoint": "project.constitution",
      "optional": false
    },
    "specify": {
      "id": "specify",
      "name": "Specify",
      "description": "Convert objectives into a structured spec with stories, requirements, scope, failure modes, and acceptance criteria.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/spec.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.spec"
    },
    "clarify": {
      "id": "clarify",
      "name": "Clarify",
      "description": "Resolve ambiguities, contradictions, and unresolved decisions in the spec before planning.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/spec.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.clarify"
    },
    "plan": {
      "id": "plan",
      "name": "Plan",
      "description": "Produce a dependency-aware implementation plan grounded in repository evidence and the spec.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/plan.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.plan"
    },
    "data-model": {
      "id": "data-model",
      "name": "Data Model",
      "description": "Define entities, relations, invariants, and API contracts implied by the spec and plan.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/data-model.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.datamodel"
    },
    "checklist": {
      "id": "checklist",
      "name": "Checklist",
      "description": "Generate quality checklists for completeness, clarity, consistency, security, and testing.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/checklist.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.checklist"
    },
    "tasks": {
      "id": "tasks",
      "name": "Tasks",
      "description": "Break the plan into actionable, tracked tasks with dependencies, estimates, and owners.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/tasks.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.tasks"
    },
    "analyze": {
      "id": "analyze",
      "name": "Analyze",
      "description": "Cross-artifact consistency analysis: spec, plan, data model, tasks, and checklist must agree.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.analyze"
    },
    "wave-plan": {
      "id": "wave-plan",
      "name": "Wave Plan",
      "description": "Generate a wave-config from structured tasks for parallel agent dispatch.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/wave-config.json",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.execute",
      "optional": true
    },
    "implement": {
      "id": "implement",
      "name": "Implement",
      "description": "Execute the approved tasks with bounded autonomy, updating artifacts as decisions change.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/tasks.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.implement"
    },
    "review": {
      "id": "review",
      "name": "Review",
      "description": "Post-implementation code review for bugs, security, quality, and spec coherence. Produces specs/<feature-id>/review.md.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/review.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.review"
    },
    "tests": {
      "id": "tests",
      "name": "Tests",
      "description": "Detect test framework, generate tests from acceptance criteria, and run them. Produces specs/<feature-id>/tests.md.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/tests.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.tests"
    },
    "lint": {
      "id": "lint",
      "name": "Lint",
      "description": "Detect linter, run it, and auto-fix fixable issues. Produces specs/<feature-id>/lint-report.md.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/lint-report.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.lint"
    },
    "security": {
      "id": "security",
      "name": "Security",
      "description": "STRIDE-driven security review of the implemented change. Produces specs/<feature-id>/security-review.md.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/security-review.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.security"
    },
    "verify": {
      "id": "verify",
      "name": "Verify",
      "description": "Run acceptance criteria, checklists, static checks, and tests independently from implementation.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.verify"
    },
    "converge": {
      "id": "converge",
      "name": "Converge",
      "description": "Gap analysis between spec/plan/tasks and actual implementation before delivery.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/convergence.md",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.converge"
    },
    "ship": {
      "id": "ship",
      "name": "Ship",
      "description": "Prepare the verified change for delivery without assuming publish authority.",
      "artifact": "specs/<feature-id>/",
      "entrypoint": "delivery.ship"
    }
  },
  "featureIdRules": {
    "maxLength": 64,
    "pattern": "^[0-9]{3}-[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$",
    "description": "Zero-padded three-digit serial number followed by a short kebab-case name, e.g. '001-native-auth', '042-batch-import'. The same ID is used for the spec directory, branch, and worktree names."
  },
  "branchAndWorktree": {
    "useFeatureId": true,
    "description": "The feature ID is the canonical branch name and worktree directory name."
  },
  "qualityGates": [
    {
      "id": "completeness",
      "name": "Completeness",
      "checks": [
        "Every requirement has an acceptance criterion.",
        "Every acceptance criterion has a verification method.",
        "All known failure modes are documented.",
        "Dependencies and blockers are explicit."
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "clarity",
      "name": "Clarity",
      "checks": [
        "User stories name a stakeholder and observable outcome.",
        "No ambiguous pronouns or undefined terms in acceptance criteria.",
        "Scope and non-goals are distinguishable."
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "consistency",
      "name": "Consistency",
      "checks": [
        "Spec, plan, data model, tasks, and checklists do not contradict each other.",
        "Terminology matches repository and architecture conventions.",
        "Stable IDs and file references are correct."
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "security",
      "name": "Security",
      "checks": [
        "Trust boundaries are identified for every affected surface.",
        "Input validation, auth, and authz are covered.",
        "No credentials or secrets are written to specs or plans."
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "tests",
      "name": "Tests",
      "checks": [
        "Each acceptance criterion maps to at least one test or check.",
        "Failure-mode tests are included where practical.",
        "Test commands are recorded and runnable."
      ]
    }
  ],
  "defaultSections": {
    "spec": [
      "user-stories",
      "requirements",
      "scope",
      "non-goals",
      "acceptance-criteria",
      "failure-modes",
      "dependencies",
      "unresolved-decisions"
    ],
    "plan": [
      "summary",
      "phases",
      "milestones",
      "stack-choices",
      "risks",
      "verification",
      "rollback"
    ],
    "data-model": [
      "entities",
      "relations",
      "invariants",
      "api-contracts",
      "migration-notes"
    ],
    "tasks": [
      "overview",
      "task-list",
      "dependencies",
      "estimates",
      "owners"
    ],
    "checklist": [
      "completeness",
      "clarity",
      "consistency",
      "security",
      "tests"
    ],
    "convergence": [
      "summary",
      "gaps",
      "resolved-decisions",
      "unresolved-decisions",
      "delivery-readiness"
    ]
  },
  "lightweightTrack": {
    "description": "A spec may substitute an approved action-plan document for plan+data-model+checklist+tasks. The spec.md MUST declare the lightweight track in its Status field and reference the substituting document. The action-plan document MUST be approved before implementation begins.",
    "substitutedPhases": [
      "plan",
      "data-model",
      "checklist",
      "tasks"
    ],
    "requiredDeclaration": "spec.md Status field must say 'lightweight track — see [document path]'",
    "gate": "The substituting document must be committed and referenced before the implement phase."
  },
  "qualityGatesNote": "qualityGates are textual checks on spec.md (static, pre-implementation). They are orthogonal to the tests/security entrypoints which run executable checks on implemented code (dynamic, post-implementation)."
}

personalized: true

<!-- ACOS-ORIENTATION:START -->
> **Orientation**: Read `.ssot/context-index.md`, `.ssot/status.md`, and

> **Bootstrap note**: If ACOS is not yet installed on this project (no
> `npx acos` available, or `.ssot/` was created by a much older version and

Treat the user's accompanying text as the current objective.

## Project-specific orientation (local-ai-packaged)

`local-ai-packaged` is a Docker Compose–based self-hosted AI stack (Ollama, Open WebUI, n8n,
Flowise, Qdrant, Neo4j, SearXNG, Langfuse, Caddy, and a custom Python MCP server) — an
**infrastructure project, not an application with a test suite**. There is no `npm test` /
`pytest` equivalent to run on resume; treat Docker Compose validity and container health as
the primary "is it working" signal instead.

- **Cheap validity check** (read-only, safe to always run): `docker compose config --quiet`
  (add `-f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.minimal.yml` or the other override combination
  named in `.ssot/status.md`/`.ssot/handoff.md` if the session concerns that variant). A
  non-zero exit means the compose graph itself is broken — surface this before anything else.
- **Live health check** (only if containers are expected to be running — do not start the
  stack yourself just to check): `docker compose ps` and `docker ps --filter
  network=ai_network` to see which services are up; do not conclude a service is broken from
  compose config alone.
- **MCP server**: source is `mcp_server/` (Python 3.11, `mcp`/`httpx`/`pydantic`/`starlette`/
  `uvicorn`, built via `Dockerfile.mcp` and `docker-bake.hcl`). If the objective touches it,
  `docker buildx bake --load` rebuilds it; there is no separate unit-test command for it.
- **Registry**: images build to `registry.lan.local:8444/local-ai-packaged/` — do not assume a
  public registry.
- **Ecosystem**: this is a **satellite** of `master-infra` (`.ssot/agents/clients.json` →
  `ecosystemParent.path: ".."`) using the shared external Docker network `ai_network`
  (`laip_ai_network` alias in compose files). Read the parent's `.ssot/status.md` for
  ecosystem-wide state (step 9 below) before assuming this project's Supabase, network, or
  registry setup is self-contained — Supabase is intentionally disabled here in favor of the
  cloud instance provisioned by `archon-v2` (see `.ssot/decisions.md`).
- **`.ssot/agents/runtimes.json`** currently only declares an example `fabric-staging` runtime
  left over from the ACOS template — it does not describe a real runtime for this project.
  Treat step 10 below as a no-op until a real runtime is declared or the stale entry is
  removed; do not run `acos-runtime-sync` against it as if it were live.

## Fast-path: automated improvement cycle

If the user's intent is to launch an automated improvement cycle (text mentions
"auto-improve", "cycle", "frontier-consult", or `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md` exists),
skip the full drift/diagnostic battery below and fast-path to the cycle:

1. Read `.ssot/handoff.md` and `.ssot/status.md` only (steps 2, 7 below — lightweight).
2. If `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md` exists: launch `0200-frontier-consult --consumer <id>`
   with the question it contains. The frontier model produces the plan, hands off to the
   consumer entrypoint (e.g. `1840-auto-improve`), which generates the wave-config and
   presents it for approval (the single human gate).
3. If no session-bridge prompt but the user named a consumer entrypoint (e.g.
   "auto-improve", "1960-auto-improve-consat"): launch `0200-frontier-consult --consumer
   <that-id>` with the user's text as the question.
4. Do NOT run version drift, structural drift, runtime drift, ecosystem drift, or
   handoff-check in fast-path mode — these are background concerns that can run after the
   cycle or on the next plain resume. The cycle is the priority.

The full procedure below runs when the user wants a plain resume (no cycle intent
detected).

## Full procedure

1. Read `.ssot/context-index.md` and `.ssot/specifications.json` to locate active specs and canonical sources.
2. Read `.ssot/handoff.md` for the "Next recommended action" and `.ssot/status.md` for the current objective, active milestone, and open items.
3. Before selecting the next action, verify the project's ACOS version is current:
   1. Read `.ssot/agents/clients.json` and extract `ssotVersion`. If the file does not exist, skip this
      step (the project is not initialized).
   2. Compare with the current ACOS code's `CURRENT_SSOT_VERSION` (from
      `scripts/core/ssot-migrations.mjs` or the installed ACOS package).
   3. If `ssotVersion < CURRENT_SSOT_VERSION`: **this is a blocker.** Surface it to the user: "Project
      ssotVersion X.Y.Z is older than ACOS version A.B.C. A migration is required before continuing."
      Route to `migration.analyze` / `1120-migrate-analyze` to perform a pre-migration analysis that
      identifies custom content at risk, missing state files, semantic references, and non-conformities
      before the deterministic apply. See `docs/migrations.md` for the full hybrid workflow procedure.
      Do not continue with other resume steps until the migration is complete or the user explicitly
      defers it.
      **After the migration apply completes, always run `npx --no-install acos --fix` to regenerate
      client projections** (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.kilo/`, etc.) from the migrated SSOT. The
      deterministic `acos-migrate --apply` updates canonical sources under `.ssot/` but does not
      regenerate projections itself — that is `acos --fix`'s responsibility. Skipping `acos --fix`
      leaves the project with stale projections that `acos --check` will flag as drift on the next
      resume. Then run `npx --no-install acos --check` to confirm no drift remains.
   4. If `ssotVersion === CURRENT_SSOT_VERSION`: run `npx acos-migrate --root . --reconcile` (dry-run)
      to check for structural drift — the version may match but the file layout may not (manual version
      bumps, partial migrations, custom entrypoint changes). If the reconcile plan reports renames,
      moves, additions, or version bumps, surface them: "Structural drift detected: N changes needed.
      This often indicates the version was bumped with `--bump-ssot-version` without running
      `acos-migrate --apply`. Run `npx acos-migrate --root . --reconcile --apply` to fix." Do not
      continue until the user resolves the drift or explicitly defers it.
      **After `--reconcile --apply` completes, always run `npx --no-install acos --fix` to regenerate
      client projections from the reconciled SSOT.** The reconcile apply updates canonical sources
      but does not regenerate projections. Then run `npx --no-install acos --check` to confirm no
      drift remains. If the user deferred the drift, flag it in `.ssot/handoff.md` so the next resume
      surfaces it again.
      **Also verify `acosSource`**: read `.ssot/agents/clients.json` → `acosSource`. If absent, warn:
      "acosSource not declared in clients.json — ACOS code path must be discovered manually. Consider
      adding acosSource to clients.json." If `type: "local-checkout"` but the path doesn't resolve to
      a valid ACOS checkout (missing `scripts/core/sync-clients.mjs`), warn: "acosSource.path does not
      point to a valid ACOS checkout. Update clients.json or restore the checkout."
   5. If `ssotVersion > CURRENT_SSOT_VERSION`: the ACOS code is outdated. Advise the user: "Project
      ssotVersion X.Y.Z is newer than this ACOS version A.B.C. Update ACOS or roll back the project."
   6. Check for core-reserved slot collisions: if the project has a custom entrypoint at order 1300,
      1320, 1340, 1360, 1380, 1400, 1420, or 1440, surface it as informational (not a blocker): "Custom entrypoint <slug> uses
      order <order>, which is reserved for ACOS core (`1300-mco-relaunch-agent`, `1320-mco-abandon-cycle`,
      `1340-mco-override-dependency`, `1360-mco-prepare-cycle`, `1380-mco-trigger-cycle`, `1400-mco-force-analysis`, `1420-mco-open-pr`, `1440-mco-authorize-merge`). Consider reclassifying or renumbering per
      `docs/specs/000-numbering-conventions/spec.md`." Do not block the resume flow.
   7. **Ecosystem version drift**: if `ecosystemRole === "container"` with `ecosystemChildren`,
      run `npx acos-migrate --root . --reconcile` (dry-run) and check the analysis artifact's
      `ecosystemVersionDrift[]` section. If any satellites are at a different `ssotVersion` than
      the container, surface them: "Ecosystem version drift detected: N satellite(s) are at a
      different version than the container: <satellite-path> (X.Y.Z vs container Z.Y.X).
      Run `npx acos-migrate --root . --ecosystem --apply` to migrate all projects atomically."
      Do not block the resume flow — this is informational unless the user is about to start
      migration work, in which case it becomes a blocker that must be resolved first.
4. If a specific spec or task is requested, read only that spec's `spec.md` and `tasks.md` rather than all specs.
5. Inspect Git status and recent history without discarding or rewriting existing changes.
6. Run the cheapest useful environment and dependency checks — for this project that is
   `docker compose config --quiet` plus, if containers are expected to be running,
   `docker compose ps` (see "Project-specific orientation" above; there is no test suite to
   run). Use `maintenance.doctor` if drift is suspected and `maintenance.infrastructure` when
   shared platform state matters (note: no `.ssot/infrastructure-profile.json` exists yet, so
   `0680-infra` will report infrastructure as unconfigured — this is expected, not a bug).
7. Compare claimed state with repository evidence and identify stale documentation or incomplete work.
   Use `npx --no-install acos-handoff-check --root .`; if it reports `review` or `stale`, follow its
   recovery evidence before trusting the recorded next action.
8. If the project declares a `gitWorktree` scope in `.ssot/agents/clients.json`, detect the current
   worktree with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. Verify the active branch and bare repository against
   the canonical declaration. If the branch mismatches or the bare repository is not at the declared
   path, report it as a blocker and do not continue until the worktree is on the expected branch or the
   declaration is updated.
9. If `.ssot/agents/clients.json` declares an `ecosystemParent`, load the parent SSOT in addition to the
   local SSOT: read the parent `.ssot/status.md`, `.ssot/handoff.md`, and `.ssot/context-index.md`. Merge
   the parent's context with the local context; prefer the local `.ssot` when the same file is declared
   in `ecosystemParent.overridden`.
10. If `.ssot/agents/runtimes.json` exists, read the latest `ACOS_RUNTIME_SYNC_REPORT.json` (if present).
   If the report shows `runtime-diverged`, stop and ask the user to reconcile git and the runtime before
   continuing; offer to run `npx --no-install acos-runtime-sync --root .` to refresh the report. Do not
   run runtime drift/health commands automatically from `0020-resume`.
11. Select the smallest next action that advances the user's objective.
12. **Check for a session-bridge prompt** — if `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md` exists, it was
    prepared by `1040-session-bridge` at the end of the previous session. Read it and show
    the user: the consumer entrypoint ID, the question, and the context summary. Ask the
    user: "A session-bridge prompt was found. Launch the automated cycle now? This will
    invoke a frontier model and consume quota." Do NOT launch anything without explicit
    user approval. If the user approves, launch `0200-frontier-consult --consumer <id>`
    with the question. After the frontier model produces the plan and the user approves,
    hand off to the consumer entrypoint with `--from-frontier`. Delete
    `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md` after the cycle is launched (one-shot — if the cycle
    fails or is interrupted, the user can re-run `1040-session-bridge` to prepare a new
    one). If the user declines, keep the file for a future session.
13. Continue directly when intent is clear; ask only when a missing decision materially changes the result.
14. Update durable status and handoff facts after meaningful progress.

Use the user's accompanying text as the complete request. This is the default single-command
orchestrator for a complete engineering cycle; never require the user to invoke each delivery
entrypoint separately.

1. Classify the request as a question, diagnosis, specification, implementation, verification, or delivery task.
2. Load only the required durable context. If project state is uncertain or stale, apply `project.resume` first without asking the user to repeat the request.
3. For a question or diagnosis, inspect evidence and answer without mutating files unless a fix was also requested.
4. If the task is ambiguous or needs structured refinement, route through the ACOS spec lifecycle: `delivery.spec` (specify/clarify), `delivery.plan`, `delivery.datamodel` (`0180-data-model`), `delivery.checklist`, then `delivery.execute` as needed.
5. For implementation work, apply `delivery.spec` to create or reconcile acceptance criteria, then apply `delivery.plan` to produce a dependency-aware plan grounded in repository evidence.
6. Present the proposed plan and pause for one explicit user approval before the first implementation mutation. Clarifications that materially change scope belong before this approval.
7. After approval, continue the same request autonomously through `delivery.execute`, `delivery.analyze`, and `delivery.verify`. Do not ask the user to re-invoke `0260-execute` or `0300-verify`.
8. After implementation and before verification, run the quality gates: `delivery.review`, `delivery.tests`, `delivery.lint`, and `delivery.security`. Skip a gate if its tool is absent (FM-001). The gate artifacts (`review.md`, `tests.md`, `lint-report.md`, `security-review.md`) feed `delivery.converge`.
9. If verification fails, diagnose and repair in scope, then re-run the relevant verification. Stop only for a product decision, missing authority, or external blocker that cannot be resolved safely.
10. Apply `delivery.converge` before `delivery.ship` to produce a gap analysis and delivery-readiness checklist. The convergence analysis incorporates the quality-gate findings.
11. Apply `delivery.ship` only to prepare delivery. Commit, push, publish, deploy, merge, or external messaging still require explicit authority.
12. Update `.ssot/status.md` and `.ssot/handoff.md` after meaningful changes, preserving exact verification evidence and residual risks.

.ssot/agents/entrypoints/0200-frontier-c.content:
---
description: Invoke a frontier model via one of the ACOS client CLIs for strategic analysis
---

<!-- ACOS-ORIENTATION:START -->
> **Orientation**: Read `.ssot/context-index.md`, `.ssot/status.md`, and
> `.ssot/handoff.md` before proceeding. Full reference:
> `.ssot/agents/context/orientation.md`.
<!-- ACOS-ORIENTATION:END -->

Invoke a frontier AI model to analyze a problem, produce a plan, or review an approach that
the current agent cannot resolve confidently. The frontier model acts as a smarter peer — it
receives the context and the question, and returns its own analysis and plan.

## When to use this

- The current agent is stuck or uncertain about an architectural decision.
- A refactor/migration deserves an independent analysis from a stronger model.
- A plan needs adversarial review before execution.
- The user explicitly asks for a frontier model's opinion.

## Philosophy — read this before building the prompt

**The frontier model is a smarter peer, not an instruction follower.** You are paying for its
reasoning capacity — if you tell it exactly what to do, you waste that capacity and get nothing
of value. The whole point is to get an **independent critical analysis** that the current agent
cannot produce itself.

**The primary pattern**: a cheaper model (Tier 1/2) produces a detailed plan → the frontier
model (Tier 3) critiques, validates, or restructures it. You send the plan + the context + the
objective, and you ask "is this plan sound? what would you change?". You do NOT send a
step-by-step specification of what the frontier model should output.

**Do**: give the frontier model the objective, the project context, the relevant files, and the
plan/approach to review. Clear variables, clear constraints, clear question.

**Don't**: inject your own analysis, tell it what the answer should be, assign it a role, dictate
output format (unless `--consumer` is set), or write a hyper-detailed prompt that over-specifies
the task. If you tell it what to think, it will react to your hypothesis instead of forming its
own — and you will have spent frontier-model quota for nothing.

## Tier routing and budget gate (mandatory)

This entrypoint is **Tier 3 (Premium)** by definition — it invokes a frontier model. Per the
global token-efficiency rules:

- **Never start here.** Tier 1 (Auto/Cascade) and Tier 2 (Named Models) MUST be attempted first
  for the task at hand. Frontier-consult is escalation only — use it after a cheaper pass has
  failed or when the user explicitly requests it.
- **Direct invocation = approval.** When the user explicitly invokes this entrypoint (e.g.
  `/0200-frontier-consult ...`), that invocation IS the authorization to consume quota. Do NOT
  ask "are you sure?" or "can I proceed?" — the user already told you to proceed. Announce
  briefly which CLI and model will be used (one line), then invoke. No gate.
- **Subagent usage.** If this entrypoint is invoked from a subagent (not a top-level user
  session), the subagent MUST obtain explicit prior approval from the user before invoking.
  Subagents cannot authorize quota consumption on their own. This is the ONLY case where you
  stop and ask — direct user invocation never requires it.
- **Token budget.** If the user has declared a token budget for the session (in
  `.ssot/status.md` or verbally), track consumption and warn when the frontier invocation
  would exceed the remaining budget. If no budget is declared, proceed without warning — the
  user knows frontier models cost quota, that's why they invoked this entrypoint.

## Inputs

The user's accompanying text is the **question**. Optionally:
- `--files <path1,path2,...>` — files to include as context (read and appended to the prompt).
- `--model <name>` — frontier model to invoke (default: `opus` → `claude --model claude-opus-4-8`).
- `--cli <name>` — which ACOS client CLI to use (default: `claude`). See "Available CLIs" below.
- `--model <name>` overrides: see `docs/agent-waves/model-selection.md` for the canonical
  model selection strategy (planification vs exécution, pricing, availability). Do not guess
  model names — read that document first.
- `--consumer <entrypoint-id>` — format the frontier model's output for direct consumption by
  the named entrypoint. See "Consumer-aware mode" below.

## Available CLIs (ACOS clients with headless mode)

The following ACOS clients have a CLI suitable for frontier-consult. The table below is the
**complete and canonical reference** — binary, Windows absolute path, prompt mode, output mode,
and the **mandatory bypass approvals + sandbox flag**. Use the bypass flag in EVERY invocation
(interactive AND headless) so the CLI never pauses to ask for approval.

| CLI | Binary | Windows absolute path | Prompt mode | Output mode | Bypass flag (MANDATORY — use every time) |
|-----|--------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------|------------------------------------------|
| Claude Code | `claude` | `%APPDATA%\npm\claude.cmd` | file (`--prompt-file`) | stdout (`-p`) | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` |
| OpenAI Codex | `codex` | `%APPDATA%\npm\codex.cmd` | positional or stdin (`codex exec - `) | stdout | `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` |
| Devin CLI | `devin` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\devin\cli\bin\devin.exe` | file (`--prompt-file`) | export-log (`--export`) | `--permission-mode dangerous` |
| Cursor | `agent` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\cursor-agent\agent.cmd` | positional (no `--prompt-file`) | stream-json | `--force` (alias `--yolo`) + `--trust` |
| Kilo Code | `kilocode` | `%APPDATA%\npm\kilocode.cmd` | positional (`--command`) | stdout | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` (or `--auto`) |
| OpenCode | `opencode` | `%APPDATA%\npm\opencode.cmd` | file (`--prompt-file`) | stdout | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` |

> **Bypass flag is MANDATORY in every invocation.** Without it, the CLI pauses on every tool call
> asking for approval — the user has to accept commands constantly. Always include the bypass flag
> from the table above, whether interactive or headless. This is non-negotiable.

### Binary discovery — mandatory procedure (do NOT skip to invocation)

**On Windows, `Get-Command <cli>` / `command -v <cli>` FAILS for most CLIs even when they are
installed.** npm global bins (`%APPDATA%\npm\`) and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\cursor-agent\` are typically
NOT in the agent's PATH. You MUST probe the absolute fallback paths. Do not conclude a CLI is
"not installed" just because `Get-Command` returned nothing.

Follow this 3-tier discovery in order. Stop at the first tier that resolves a usable binary:

**Tier 1 — PATH lookup (fast but unreliable on Windows):**
```powershell
Get-Command claude,codex,devin,agent,kilocode,opencode -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Select-Object Name, Source
```
On Linux/macOS: `command -v claude codex devin agent kilocode opencode 2>/dev/null`

**Tier 2 — Windows absolute path probe (mandatory when Tier 1 finds nothing):**
```powershell
$candidates = @{
  claude    = @("$env:APPDATA\npm\claude.cmd")
  codex     = @("$env:APPDATA\npm\codex.cmd", "$env:APPDATA\npm\codex.ps1")
  devin     = @("$env:LOCALAPPDATA\devin\cli\bin\devin.exe")
  agent     = @("$env:LOCALAPPDATA\cursor-agent\agent.cmd")
  kilocode  = @("$env:APPDATA\npm\kilocode.cmd")
  opencode  = @("$env:APPDATA\npm\opencode.cmd")
}
foreach ($cli in $candidates.Keys) {
  foreach ($p in $candidates[$cli]) {
    if (Test-Path $p) { Write-Output "FOUND: $cli -> $p"; break }
  }
}
```
Use the resolved absolute path as the binary for invocation (e.g. `& "$env:APPDATA\npm\codex.cmd"
exec ...` instead of `codex exec ...`).

**Tier 3 — project overlay (machine-specific paths):**
If the project has an agent-waves overlay file (e.g. `docs/agent-waves-overlay-<project>.md`),
read it for the machine-specific `DEVIN_BIN`, `CURSOR_BIN`, `OPENCODE_BIN` variables. These
override the Tier 2 defaults when present.

**If all three tiers fail for a CLI**: that CLI is genuinely not installed. Report it to the user
with the install command (see links below) and fall back to the next available CLI from the table.

### Model selection — read before choosing a model

The golden rule: **invest in thinking (expensive models), save on execution (free/cheap models).**
This entrypoint is Tier 3 (frontier consult) — by default you want a planning-grade model, not
an execution-grade one. But the user may override.

Quick reference (canonical — do not guess model names):

| Use case | Model class | Examples (API ID) |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **Architecture, migration strategy, critical analysis** | Top-tier planning | `claude-opus-4-8`, `gpt-5.6-terra` |
| **Standard planning, spec review, capture d'essence** | 2nd-tier planning | `claude-sonnet-5`, `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| **Execution of already-planned tasks** | Free/economic | `glm-5.2`, `kimi-k2-7` (Devin CLI + sous-agents `run_subagent`) — **jamais Haiku, jamais GPT 5.4** |

**Do not guess model names.** If unsure, ask the user which model to use rather than inventing an
API ID. Model names change frequently; the table above is the canonical reference embedded in this
entrypoint.

### Launch modes (interactive is the default)

Each CLI supports two launch modes:

- **Interactive** (default for frontier-consult): visible in a terminal pane (Windows Terminal
  `wt.exe` or `tmux` on Linux/WSL) for human supervision. Drops headless-only flags (e.g. Cursor
  drops `-p`, `--trust`, `--output-format`; Claude drops `-p`; Codex uses `codex` not `codex exec`).
  This is the default because frontier-consult produces analysis that the user needs to read and
  judge — running it in a visible pane lets the user follow the reasoning in real time and
  continue the conversation after the initial response. **The bypass flag is STILL included in
  interactive mode** — without it the CLI pauses on every tool call.
- **Headless** (opt-in, for automated pipelines only): non-interactive, captures stdout/export-log
  to a file. Used by `wave-dispatch.mjs --mode cli-headless` and when the frontier model's output
  is consumed by another entrypoint (`--consumer` mode) without human review. **Do not use
  headless as the default** — it hides the frontier model's reasoning from the user.

For interactive mode, wrap the invocation in `wt new-tab` (Windows) or `tmux new-session`
(Linux/WSL). The wrappers below are copy-paste ready and include the bypass flag.

**Windows Terminal interactive wrappers (copy-paste ready — bypass flag included in every one):**

wt new-tab --title "Claude" --startingDirectory "$workdir" `
  cmd /k "chcp 65001 >nul & & '%APPDATA%\npm\claude.cmd' --model claude-opus-4-8 --dangerously-skip-permissions"

# Codex — interactive + bypass (no subcommand = interactive TUI; --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox)
wt new-tab --title "Codex" --startingDirectory "$workdir" `
  cmd /k "chcp 65001 >nul & & '%APPDATA%\npm\codex.cmd' -m gpt-5.6-terra --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust"

# Devin CLI — interactive + bypass (--permission-mode dangerous = auto-approve all tools)
$devin = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\devin\cli\bin\devin.exe"
wt new-tab --title "Devin" --startingDirectory "$workdir" `
  cmd /k "& '$devin' --model kimi-k2-7 --permission-mode dangerous --prompt-file '$stage\prompt.md' --export '$stage\export.jsonl'"

# Cursor agent — interactive + bypass (--force = auto-approve, --trust = skip workspace trust)
wt new-tab --title "Cursor" --startingDirectory "$workdir" `
  cmd /k "& '$env:LOCALAPPDATA\cursor-agent\agent.cmd' --model auto --force --trust --workspace $workdir"

## Consumer-aware mode (`--consumer <entrypoint-id>`)

When `--consumer <entrypoint-id>` is provided, the frontier model's plan is structured for
direct consumption by the named entrypoint. This enables the pattern: **frontier model plans
(expensive) → consumer entrypoint executes (cheap models)**.

### How it works

1. **Resolve the consumer entrypoint**: look up `<entrypoint-id>` in `.ssot/agents/workflows.json`
   (by stable ID or source filename), then read the corresponding file in
   `.ssot/agents/entrypoints/`.
2. **Read the `planConsumer` section from its frontmatter**: if present, it contains:
   - `specPath` — where to persist the plan (e.g. `"specs/auto-improve-{date}/"`)
   - `planFile` — the filename (e.g. `"tasks.md"`)
   - `planFormat` — the exact format the consumer expects (a YAML multi-line string)
   - `{date}` is replaced with today's date (YYYY-MM-DD).
3. **If no `planConsumer` section**: fall back to the default advisory format and warn the
   user that the consumer entrypoint does not declare a plan consumer.
4. **If `planConsumer` is present**: add the planFormat to the prompt as a format constraint
   on the plan section only (see step 4 of the procedure).
5. **After invocation** (step 7): in addition to `docs/prompts/<timestamp>-...-output.md`,
   persist the plan to `<specPath>/<planFile>` (creating directories as needed).
6. **Gate**: present the plan to the user for approval (step 8). After approval, hand off to
   the consumer entrypoint. The consumer detects the pre-existing plan file and skips its own
   planning phases — this is the consumer's responsibility to implement (typically via a
   `--from-frontier` flag or by checking if the plan file already exists).

### What the consumer declares (project-specific, not ACOS source)

The consumer entrypoint's frontmatter is project-owned. ACOS source does not hardcode any
consumer. Any entrypoint (ACOS source or project custom) can declare a `planConsumer` section:

```yaml
planConsumer:
  specPath: "specs/auto-improve-{date}/"
  planFile: "tasks.md"
  planFormat: |
    - [ ] **T-001** — <description>
      - Depends on: none
      - Files: `<path>`
      - Domain: code|tests|docs|infra
      - Parallelizable: true|false
      - Lane: A1
```

The `planFormat` is injected verbatim into the frontier model's prompt. The consumer is
responsible for parsing and executing the plan file it receives.

## Procedure

1. **Detect available CLIs** — follow the 3-tier "Binary discovery" procedure in the
   "Available CLIs" section above. **Do NOT use `command -v <cli>` alone** — on Windows it
   fails for most CLIs even when installed. Probe the absolute fallback paths (Tier 2) before
   concluding a CLI is missing. If the requested CLI is not found after all 3 tiers, fall back
   to the next available from the table. If none are available, stop and tell the user to
   install one (see links above). Record the resolved binary path — use it as the absolute path
   for invocation (e.g. `& "$env:APPDATA\npm\codex.cmd" exec ...` not `codex exec ...`).

2. **Self-skip check** — if the current agent is already running on the requested frontier
   model, skip the external invocation and answer directly (invoking yourself is wasteful).
   Detect the current agent by checking environment variables for each client:
   - Claude: `CLAUDE_MODEL` or `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`
   - Devin: `DEVIN_MODEL` or session metadata
   - Cursor: `CURSOR_MODEL`
   - Codex: `CODEX_MODEL` or `OPENAI_MODEL`
   - Kilo: `KILO_MODEL`
   - OpenCode: `OPENCODE_MODEL`
   If unsure which model the current agent is running on, skip the self-skip check and just
   invoke the frontier model — a redundant invocation is cheaper than a blocked one.

3. **Announce and proceed** — state in one line which CLI and model will be used (e.g.
   "Invoking Codex (gpt-5.6-terra) with 3 context files..."), then proceed immediately to
   build the prompt and invoke. **Do NOT ask for approval** — the user's invocation of this
   entrypoint is the approval. The only exception is subagent invocation (see "Tier routing
   and budget gate" above), which requires explicit prior user approval.

4. **Gather context** — this is the most important step. The quality of the frontier model's
   output depends almost entirely on the quality of the context you provide. Spend your time
   here, not on formatting instructions.

   - **Read the project context**: `.ssot/context-index.md`, `.ssot/status.md`,
     `.ssot/handoff.md`. If the question is architectural, also read `.ssot/constitution.md`
     and `.ssot/architecture.md`. If a feature ID is active, read the active
     `spec.md`/`plan.md`/`tasks.md`.
   - **Select relevant files**: if `--files` provided, use those. If not, select the files
     most relevant to the question (max 5 by default; prefer `.ssot/`
     canonical sources over generated projections; summarize files >500 lines instead of
     including full content). Exclude files matching `.env*`, `*credential*`, `*secret*`,
     `*token*` (see Authority).
   - **Do NOT inject your own analysis or hypotheses.** The whole point of consulting a
     frontier model is to get an independent perspective. If you tell it what you think the
     answer is, it will react to your hypothesis instead of forming its own. Send the
     question and the context — let the frontier model do the thinking.

5. **Build the prompt** — keep it minimal. The prompt is:

   ```
   <the user's question, verbatim>

   ---

   ## Project context

   <relevant sections of context-index.md, status.md, handoff.md, architecture.md, etc.>

   ## Files

   <file contents, each under a ## File: <path> heading>
   ```

   That's it. No role assignment, no directives, no output contract, no sub-agent
   delegation instructions, no budget lectures. The frontier model is smart — let it
   decide how to structure its response.

   **If `--consumer` was provided and a `planConsumer` section was found**: add one line
   after the question:

   ```
   Produce the plan section in this exact format (it will be consumed by
   <entrypoint-id>):
   <planFormat>
   ```

   This is the only case where you constrain the output format. Without `--consumer`, let
   the frontier model structure its response however it judges best.

6. **Write the prompt to a persistent file** — `docs/prompts/<timestamp>-<cli>-<slug>.md`
   where `<timestamp>` is UTC `YYYY-MM-DDTHH-MM-SSZ`, `<cli>` is the client CLI used, and
   `<slug>` is a short kebab-case description of the question. Use a file (not stdin inline)
   to avoid shell-quoting issues with multi-line markdown. **Do not write to `/tmp/** — the
   prompt is an auditable artifact and must be persisted alongside the output.

7. **Prompt file persisted** — the prompt is saved at
   `docs/prompts/<timestamp>-<cli>-<slug>.md`. State the path in one line so the user can
   review it if they want. **Do NOT block invocation waiting for review** — proceed to
   invoke immediately. The user can read the prompt file after the fact or interrupt if they
   disagree with the context selection.

8. **Invoke the frontier model** — use the CLI's **interactive mode** (default) with a
   Windows Terminal wrapper (`wt new-tab`) or `tmux` on Linux/WSL. Use the copy-paste wrappers
   in the "Windows Terminal interactive wrappers" section above. The frontier model's reasoning
   is visible to the user in real time.
   - **Headless opt-in**: only use headless mode (`codex exec`, `claude -p`, etc.) when
     `--consumer` is set (automated pipeline, no human review needed) or the user explicitly
     requests it. In headless mode, run synchronously and capture stdout to
     `docs/prompts/<timestamp>-<cli>-<slug>-output.md`.
   - In interactive mode, after the session ends, save the output to
     `docs/prompts/<timestamp>-<cli>-<slug>-output.md` for the audit trail.

9. **Read the output** — read the output file and present the frontier model's answer to the
   user.
   **If `--consumer` was NOT provided**: this is a standalone consultation. Present the
   answer. Do not execute anything — the user decides what to do with the advice.
   **If `--consumer` was provided**: the frontier model's plan is an intermediate artifact.
   The consumer entrypoint (e.g. `1840-auto-improve`) will generate the final wave-config
   and present IT for approval (that is the single human gate). Do NOT pause here — hand
   off immediately to the consumer entrypoint (e.g. `/devin:<consumer-id> --from-frontier`).
   The consumer detects the pre-existing plan file and skips its own diagnostic/planning
   phases. The user approves the wave plan at the consumer's gate, not here.

10. **Persist the artifact** — if a feature ID is active, also write a copy of the output to
    `specs/<feature-id>/frontier-consult-<timestamp>.md` (or `docs/specs/<feature-id>/` if
    that is the project's spec location). Otherwise keep the output in `docs/prompts/`.
    The persisted artifact MUST include: the prompt file path, the CLI used, the model, the
    timestamp, and the full response.
    **If `--consumer` was provided and a `planConsumer` section was found**: additionally
    persist the plan to `<specPath>/<planFile>` (creating directories as needed). Extract
    the Plan section from the frontier model's output and write it as the plan file content.
    This is the file the consumer entrypoint will read to execute the plan.

11. **No cleanup** — do not delete the prompt file. Both the prompt and the output are
    persisted in `docs/prompts/` for auditability and reproducibility.

## Authority

- This entrypoint is **read-only** — it invokes an external CLI that reads files and produces
  text. It does not mutate the project.
- The frontier model's output is advisory. The current agent does not execute the plan.
  In standalone mode (no `--consumer`), the user decides what to do with the advice. In
  `--consumer` mode, the consumer entrypoint generates the final wave plan and presents
  THAT for approval — the frontier output is an intermediate artifact, not the approval
  point.
- Do not send secrets, credentials, or `.env` contents to the frontier model. If `--files`
  includes a file that looks like it contains secrets (`.env*`, `*credential*`, `*secret*`,
  `*token*`), stop and ask the user before including it.

## Self-skip

If the current agent is already running on the requested frontier model, skip the external
invocation and answer directly. Detect via the environment variables listed in step 2 of the
procedure. If unsure, skip the self-skip optimization and just invoke — a redundant call is
cheaper than blocking. This applies to all ACOS client CLIs, not just Claude.

## Relationship to agent waves

This entrypoint MAY be used as a single-agent wave step (per `docs/agent-waves/04-RUNBOOK.md`).
When used inside a wave:
- The wave-config generator MUST mark this step as `tier: 3` and `quota-consuming: true`.
- The wave MUST obtain user approval before executing this step (this is the subagent case —
  wave steps are not direct user invocations, so the budget gate applies).
- The output file path MUST be recorded in the wave status JSON so downstream agents can read
  the frontier model's recommendation.
- This entrypoint MUST NOT be parallelized with itself in the same wave (one frontier
  invocation at a time to control cost).

---
description: Prepare the next session prompt for an automated improvement cycle
---

<!-- ACOS-ORIENTATION:START -->
> **Orientation**: Read `.ssot/context-index.md`, `.ssot/status.md`, and
> `.ssot/handoff.md` before proceeding. Full reference:
> `.ssot/agents/context/orientation.md`.
<!-- ACOS-ORIENTATION:END -->

Run this **after** `1020-handoff` at the end of a session. It prepares a prompt file that
`0020-resume` will find at the start of the next session and use to launch an automated
improvement cycle: frontier model plans → consumer entrypoint executes.

## The chain

```
End of current session:
  1020-handoff        → writes status.md + handoff.md
  1030-session-bridge → writes .ssot/next-session-prompt.md

Next session:
  0020-resume         → finds next-session-prompt.md → launches the cycle
  0200 --consumer <id> → frontier model (Codex, Opus, etc.) produces the plan
  consumer --from-frontier → cheap models execute the plan
```

## Inputs

- `--consumer <entrypoint-id>` (required) — the entrypoint that will execute the plan
  produced by the frontier model. Must declare a `planConsumer` section in its frontmatter.
- `--question <text>` (optional) — the question for the frontier model. If not provided,
  the skill derives it from the handoff's "Next recommended action".

## Procedure

1. **Verify handoff exists** — read `.ssot/handoff.md`. If it's missing or empty, stop and
   tell the user to run `1020-handoff` first.

2. **Read the next action** — extract the "Next recommended action" from `.ssot/handoff.md`
   and the current objective from `.ssot/status.md`.

3. **Build the question** — if `--question` was provided, use it verbatim. Otherwise,
   reformulate the handoff's next action as an open-ended question for the frontier model.
   The question should describe **what** needs to be done, not **how** — the frontier model
   decides how. For example:
   - Handoff says: "Next: fix the 8 KPIs in ERROR state"
   - Question becomes: "Diagnose the 8 KPIs currently in ERROR state and produce a
     correction plan"

4. **Verify the consumer** — resolve `--consumer <entrypoint-id>` in
   `.ssot/agents/workflows.json`, read the entrypoint file, and confirm it has a
   `planConsumer` section in its frontmatter. If not, stop and tell the user: "Consumer
   <id> does not declare a planConsumer section. The frontier model's output won't be
   consumable by this entrypoint."

5. **Write the prompt file** — write `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md` with this structure:

   ```markdown
   # Next session — automated improvement cycle

   ## Action
   Launch `0200-frontier-consult --consumer <entrypoint-id>` with the question below.

   ## Consumer
   <entrypoint-id>

   ## Question
   <the question from step 3>

   ## Context summary
   <2-3 lines from status.md: current objective, active milestone, key blockers>

   ## After frontier-consult
   The frontier model will produce a plan. After user approval, hand off to
   `<entrypoint-id> --from-frontier` to execute with cheap models.
   ```

6. **Tell the user** — report:
   - The prompt file path (`.ssot/next-session-prompt.md`)
   - The consumer entrypoint that will be used
   - The question that will be sent to the frontier model
   - "At the next session, 0020-resume will find this prompt and launch the cycle
     automatically."

## What 0020-resume does with this file

When `0020-resume` runs at the start of the next session, it checks for
`.ssot/next-session-prompt.md`. If found, it:
1. Reads the consumer ID and question
2. Launches `0200-frontier-consult --consumer <id>` with the question
3. After the frontier model produces the plan and the user approves, hands off to the
   consumer entrypoint with `--from-frontier`
4. Deletes `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md` after the cycle is launched (one-shot)

This is a one-shot mechanism. The prompt file is consumed and deleted. If the cycle fails
or is interrupted, the user can re-run `1030-session-bridge` to prepare a new one.

## Authority

- This entrypoint is **read-only** — it writes only `.ssot/next-session-prompt.md`.
- It does not invoke the frontier model. That happens in the next session via `0200`.
- It does not execute the plan. That happens via the consumer entrypoint.

You are an autonomous agent performing a migration. **You decide, you don't ask.**

- **DO**: Read the codebase, analyze legacy files, compare with the template, and make informed
  decisions about entrypoint classification, skill audit, client rule audit, and canonical
  mappings. You have the full project context — use it.

## Ecosystem setup (container + satellites)

An ecosystem is a container project with one or more satellite sub-projects. Each project has its
own independent `.ssot/`, but they share the ACOS code location and optionally some canonical files.

### How to set up an ecosystem

1. **Install ACOS in the container** (this entrypoint, steps 1-14 above).
2. **Configure the container** — in `.ssot/agents/clients.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "ecosystemRole": "container",
     "ecosystemChildren": [
       { "path": "api", "role": "satellite" },
       { "path": "web", "role": "satellite" }
     ]
   }
   ```
3. **Install ACOS in each satellite** — run `acos init --adopt` in each sub-project directory.
4. **Configure each satellite** — in the satellite's `.ssot/agents/clients.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "ecosystemRole": "satellite",
     "ecosystemParent": {
       "path": "..",
       "inherited": [".ssot/agents/context/AGENTS.src.md"],
       "overridden": [".ssot/agents/context/CLAUDE.src.md"]
     }
   }
   ```
5. **Run `acos --fix` on each satellite** — this propagates `acosSource` from the container and copies inherited files.

### What is shared vs independent

| | Container | Satellite |
|---|-----------|-----------|
| `.ssot/` | Own, complete | Own, complete (independent) |
| `acosSource` (code ACOS) | Declared here | **Inherited automatically** — no `node_modules` needed in satellite |
| `inherited` files | Source of truth | Copied from container at each `acos --fix` (edits overwritten) |
| `overridden` files | Not propagated | Satellite manages its own version |
| Entrypoints, workflows, status, decisions | Own | Own (fully independent) |
| Projections (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, etc.) | Own | Own (fully independent) |

**Key points:**
- Each satellite is a complete ACOS project with its own `.ssot/`. The ecosystem relationship only
  controls which canonical files are synchronized from the container.
- `acosSource` is propagated automatically — satellites don't need their own `node_modules` or
  `package.json` with `@acos/core`. They use the container's ACOS code.
- `inherited: []` makes a satellite 100% independent (only shares `acosSource`).
- A file cannot be in both `inherited` and `overridden` — `240-doctor` verifies this.

### Ecosystem migration

If the target project is a **container** (`.ssot/agents/clients.json` has `ecosystemRole: "container"` with `ecosystemChildren`), the migration affects all satellites too:

- **Batch migration**: use `acos-migrate --root <container-root> --ecosystem --apply` to migrate the container and all satellites atomically. Without `--ecosystem`, only the container is migrated — satellites must be migrated individually.
- **Version drift detection**: run `acos-migrate --root <container-root> --reconcile` (dry-run) to check for structural drift across the ecosystem. The migration-analysis scanner reports `ecosystemVersionDrift[]` entries when satellites are at a different version than the container.
- **Migration order**: the container is always migrated first, then satellites in sequence. If a satellite migration fails, remaining satellites are still attempted (best-effort) so the operator can fix the failing one without re-running everything.

For the full ecosystem migration procedure, use `1180-migrate-ecosystem` which orchestrates the batch with per-project status reporting.

## Reconciliation mode (--reconcile)

The `--reconcile` flag performs structural reconciliation between a project's SSOT state and the canonical ACOS template, independent of version-based migrations. It detects:

- **Missing template entrypoints**: entrypoints present in the template but absent from the project.
- **Stale template content**: template-sourced entrypoints whose file content has drifted from the template (e.g. the project was created from an older template version). With `--apply`, these files are refreshed to the current template content. Custom entrypoints (orphans) are never touched.
- **Orphaned custom entrypoints**: project-specific entrypoints not in the template — preserved, never deleted. Those colliding with template orders are renumbered to 1500+.
- **Target configuration drift**: projection targets in `workflows.json` that differ from the template.
- **Slug collisions**: custom entrypoints whose slug collides with a template entrypoint — auto-resolvable with `--resolve-slug-collisions`.

Run `acos-migrate --root . --reconcile` for a dry-run plan, then `acos-migrate --root . --reconcile --apply` to execute. Pass `--help` to see all available options.

After reconciliation, run `acos --fix` to regenerate projections, then run the final verification script above.

### Non-destructive reconcile rules (Bug 9/10 safeguards)

The hybrid method is **non-destructive by design**. The deterministic engine handles mechanics, but
the agent is responsible for ensuring no custom content is lost. These rules apply to both
`--apply` (migration) and `--reconcile --apply` (reconciliation) paths:

1. **templateRemoved entries**: The dry-run report lists entrypoints that were once in the ACOS
   template but have been removed (e.g. `project.task`, `session.knowledge*`). The engine uses an
   explicit `REMOVED_TEMPLATE_IDS` registry — not a heuristic — so false positives are impossible.
   However, before approving `--apply`, the agent MUST:
   - Review each `templateRemoved` entry in the dry-run report.
   - If an entry is a legitimate custom (not in `REMOVED_TEMPLATE_IDS`), add its ID to the preserve
     list before applying. The engine will renumber it to 1500+ instead of deleting it.
   - If an entry IS in `REMOVED_TEMPLATE_IDS` but the project has custom content in its file that
     should be preserved, extract the custom content to a snapshot under
     `.acos/migrations/snapshots/` before applying. After apply, re-integrate the custom content
     into the appropriate replacement entrypoint (e.g. `project.task` content → `project.route`).

2. **staleTemplateContent refresh**: The engine refreshes only the **frontmatter description**
   (template-owned) and preserves the **body** (which may contain project-specific customizations).
   This is a frontmatter-only refresh, NOT a full-file overwrite. The agent should:
   - Review the dry-run report's `staleTemplateContent` section.
   - If a file's body contains custom sections that would be lost by a full overwrite (pre-Bug 10
     behavior), rest assured: the current engine only touches the frontmatter description.
   - If the frontmatter description has been intentionally customized in the project, extract it
     to a snapshot before applying, then re-apply the customization after the refresh.

3. **Pre-apply content audit (mandatory for reconcile)**: Before running `--reconcile --apply`,
   the agent MUST compare each `staleTemplateContent` file with its template counterpart and
   classify each as:
   - **template-stale**: the file matches an old template version (no custom content) → safe to
     refresh frontmatter.
   - **custom-content**: the file has project-specific sections in the body → frontmatter refresh
     is safe, body is preserved. No action needed beyond the dry-run review.
   - **mixed**: the file has both template-stale frontmatter AND custom body content → frontmatter
     refresh is safe, body is preserved. Document the custom sections in the analysis artifact.

4. **Dry-run is mandatory**: Never run `--apply` or `--reconcile --apply` without first reviewing
   the dry-run report. The report shows:
   - `Template-removed entrypoints` — entries that will be DELETED (with ⚠ warning).
   - `Stale template content` — entries whose frontmatter will be refreshed (body preserved).
   - `Orphans` — custom entrypoints that will be preserved (never deleted).

1. Run the deterministic apply:
   - `npx acos-migrate --root . --apply`
   - This writes a content-complete backup under `.acos/migrations/` (with before/after SHA-256 hashes) and then performs the route: renames entrypoint files, updates `workflows.json`, `clients.json`, `dependencies.json`, and other SSOT-bearing documents, adds new canonical files, and applies custom renumbering per the analysis. A partial apply attempts to restore already-written files from the in-memory pre-migration state.
2. Regenerate projections from the migrated SSOT:
   - `npx acos --fix`
   - This writes the projected client files (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.kilo/`, etc.) to match the new SSOT state.
3. **Gate 3 — Apply completion**: Present the migration summary to the user:
   - renames performed (old prefix → new prefix, stable ID);
   - additions (new canonical files added);
   - renumbering (custom entrypoints moved, old order → new order, reason);
   - version bump (old `ssotVersion` → new `ssotVersion`);
   - backup location (`.acos/migrations/<timestamp>/`);

  are relevant, human-approval gate interaction, and decision-logging narrative. The agent
  reads the actual code, understands what the project does, identifies what the SSOT is
  missing or gets wrong, and proposes improvements grounded in that understanding.
- **Deterministic layer** (the script `scripts/audit/ssot-personalization.mjs`): codebase
  scanning, stack detection, architecture classification, SSOT item reading, recommendation
  structuring, report generation, apply/rollback, decision logging. All mechanical, reproducible,
  offline. No network, no LLM. The script is a **complement** to the agent's understanding —
  it catches what the agent might miss mechanically, but it does not replace semantic judgment.

The agent never writes canonical SSOT sources directly — it calls the script's
`applyRecommendations()` function, which is deterministic.

## Procedure

### Phase 0 — Deep project understanding (agent, read-only)

Before any analysis or recommendations, the agent must **understand the project as a
developer would**. This is not optional — without this, personalization is generic noise.

#### 0a. Read the codebase

Read the project's actual source files — not just `.ssot/` metadata. At minimum:

- The entry point(s): `package.json` scripts, `pyproject.toml` entry points, `main.*`,
  `__main__.py`, `index.*`, or equivalent.
- The core modules: read the 3–5 most important source files that implement the project's
  primary logic. Use `grep`/`glob` to find them if not obvious.
- The test files: understand what is tested and how.
- The config files: `.env.example`, `config.*`, `*.yaml`, `*.toml` — understand the
  runtime configuration surface.
- The build/deploy files: `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.*`, CI configs, Makefile.

#### 0b. Understand what the project does

Form a mental model and write it down internally:

- **Purpose**: What does this project do? Who uses it? What problem does it solve?
- **Architecture**: How is the code organized? What are the main modules and how do they
  interact? Is it a library, a CLI, a service, a pipeline, a satellite in an ecosystem?
- **Stack**: Language(s), frameworks, key dependencies, database, external services.
- **Conventions**: Naming, error handling, logging, testing patterns, commit style.
- **Ecosystem role**: Is this a standalone project, a container, or a satellite? Does it
  have a parent? Children? Siblings it coordinates with?
- **Active state**: What is the current objective (from `.ssot/status.md`)? What is blocking
  or in progress (from `.ssot/handoff.md`)?

#### 0c. Understand the existing SSOT and client surfaces

Read and assess every SSOT item against what you now know about the project:

- **`.ssot/agents/context/AGENTS.src.md`** — Does it accurately describe the project? Is the
  architecture section correct? Are the conventions real or template boilerplate? Are there
  project-specific constraints (auth patterns, external services, data flows) that are missing?
- **`.ssot/agents/rules/common.md`** — Are the rules relevant to this project? Are there rules
  that contradict the project's actual conventions? Are there project-specific rules that
  should exist but don't (e.g. Fabric auth, SQL patterns, API contracts)?
- **`.ssot/agents/clients.json`** — Which clients are configured? Are the projections correct?
  Are there clients configured that the project doesn't use? Are there clients the project
  uses but that aren't configured?
- **`.ssot/protected-paths.json`** — Are the protected paths accurate? Are there project-specific
  files that should be protected but aren't?
- **`.ssot/constitution.md`** — Does the constitution reflect the project's actual principles
  and constraints? Or is it generic template text?
- **Entrypoints** — Read the custom entrypoints (order ≥600 or IDs with project-specific
  prefixes). Do they describe real workflows that match the codebase? Are there workflows
  the project actually needs that don't have entrypoints? Are there entrypoints that describe
  obsolete workflows?

For each client surface (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.devin/`, `.kilo/`, `.opencode/`, `.codex/`):
- Read the projected skills, rules, and config.
- Assess: does this projection give an agent working in this client enough context to be
  productive? What's missing? What's misleading?

#### 0d. Identify needs and gaps

Based on 0a–0c, write down:

1. **What the SSOT gets right** — items that accurately reflect the project. Don't touch these.
2. **What the SSOT gets wrong** — items that contradict the actual codebase or are stale
   template boilerplate that doesn't apply. These need correction.
3. **What the SSOT is missing** — project-specific knowledge, rules, context, or entrypoints
   that would make an agent more effective but don't exist. These need addition.
4. **Client surface gaps** — for each client, what would make the projection more useful?
   Missing skills? Rules that don't project correctly? Config that's wrong for the project's
   actual tooling?

This needs assessment is the **primary input** to personalization. The deterministic script
is a secondary input that catches mechanical gaps the agent might overlook.

---

### Phase 1 — Deterministic analysis (complement to Phase 0)

Run the deterministic analysis script to produce a structured `ProjectAnalysis`:

```
npx acos-personalize --root . --json
```

If the user passes `--focus <csv>`, forward it to limit analysis categories (valid values:
`context`, `rules`, `clients`, `entrypoints`, `constitution`). If the user passes `--dry-run`,
note it — no files will be modified.

If the script exits with code 2 (FM-001 — not ACOS-initialized), direct the user to `0000-new`
or `1100-migrate` and stop.

**Merge the script's findings with your Phase 0 needs assessment.** The script catches
mechanical issues (stack detection, schema validation, missing fields). Your Phase 0 assessment
catches semantic issues (wrong descriptions, missing project-specific rules, stale context).
Both matter. Deduplicate where they overlap.

---

### Phase 2 — Client best-practices research (agent layer)

If `--refresh-best-practices` was requested, or if any client's best-practices cache is stale
(older than 90 days) or missing, use `web_search` to research current best practices for each
of the 6 required clients:

- **Claude Code** (`claude`) — search for current Claude Code skills, rules, hooks, and MCP config
  patterns.
- **Cursor** (`cursor`) — search for current Cursor rules, commands, skills, and hooks patterns.
- **Devin** (`devin`) — search for current Devin CLI skills, config, and hooks patterns.
- **Kilo Code** (`kilocode`) — search for current Kilo Code skills, commands, workflows, and rules.
- **OpenCode** (`opencode`) — search for current OpenCode commands, skills, rules, and agents.
- **OpenAI Codex** (`codex`) — search for current Codex agents, hooks, and config patterns.

Write the refreshed cache to `docs/client-best-practices/<client>.md` with frontmatter
(`client`, `lastResearched`, `sourceUrls[]`) and a body of structured best practices. The cache
ships with the ACOS npm package as a shared baseline; consumer projects override locally.

If web search fails for a client, keep the existing cache and mark it `stale: true` (FM-002).
Do not crash — graceful degradation.

**Cross-reference best practices with your Phase 0 client-surface assessment.** A best practice
is only a recommendation if it's relevant to this project. Don't propose a Docker skill for a
project that has no Dockerfile. Don't propose a Cursor hook for a project where the team uses
Devin. Filter by what you learned in Phase 0.

---

### Phase 3 — Present the report

Generate `ACOS_PERSONALIZATION_REPORT.md` at the project root. The report must include:

1. **Project understanding summary** — what the project does, its architecture, its stack,
   its ecosystem role. This proves the agent read the code and isn't generating generic noise.
2. **Needs assessment** — the 4 categories from Phase 0d (right, wrong, missing, client gaps),
   with specific file references and concrete descriptions of what's off.
3. **Deterministic findings** — the script's mechanical findings, merged with the needs assessment.
4. **Client best-practices gaps** — only the ones relevant to this project (filtered by Phase 0).
5. **Proposed changes grouped by category** — each proposal must reference the specific need it
   addresses. No generic "add a rule about testing" — instead "add a rule about pytest fixture
   scope because the project uses session-scoped fixtures in tests/conftest.py and the current
   rules don't mention it."

---

### Phase 4 — Approval gate

Present the proposed changes grouped by category and ask the user to approve or reject each
group (or all/none). The approval structure is:

```
{ approved: Recommendation[], rejected: Recommendation[] }
```

- **FM-006** (all rejected): write the report with "no changes applied" and exit cleanly.
- Recommendations with `conflictsWith` set (contradicting an existing `D-xxx` decision) are
  automatically excluded from the apply step and noted in the report (FM-003).
- Recommendations with `preservesCustomization: true` are automatically skipped and noted in the
  report (INV-004).

---

### Phase 5 — Apply approved changes

For each approved recommendation, call the script's `applyRecommendations(approved, root)`
function. This:

- Modifies **only** canonical SSOT sources (INV-003 whitelist): `.ssot/agents/context/*.src.md`,
  `.ssot/agents/rules/common.md`, `.ssot/agents/clients.json`, `.ssot/protected-paths.json`,
  `.ssot/constitution.md`, and entrypoint files.
- Takes an in-memory backup before any write.
- Never edits projection files directly.

---

### Phase 6 — Regenerate projections

After all approved mutations, run `acos --fix` to regenerate projections. If `acos --fix` fails
(FM-004), the script rolls back all canonical-source changes from the in-memory backup and
reports the failure with error output. Do not proceed if rollback occurred.

---

### Phase 7 — Log decisions

For each applied recommendation, the script appends a `D-xxx` entry to `.ssot/decisions.md`
with the recommendation ID, category, file, section, rationale, and `appliedAt` timestamp. Use
the next available D number.

---

### Phase 8 — Update report

Update `ACOS_PERSONALIZATION_REPORT.md` with the applied status for each recommendation.

---

### Phase 9 — Gitignore the report (first run only)

On first run, add `ACOS_PERSONALIZATION_REPORT.md` to the project's `.gitignore` (or create one
if none exists). The report is a transient artifact (DD-009-007); durable decisions are in
`.ssot/decisions.md`.

## Flags

- `--dry-run` — produce the report and plan without modifying any files. Verified by clean Git
  status afterward.
- `--focus <csv>` — comma-separated categories: `context`, `rules`, `clients`, `entrypoints`,
  `constitution`. Default is all categories.
- `--refresh-best-practices` — triggers the agent-layer web search to refresh the client
  best-practices cache. Without this flag, the script reads the existing cache (offline).

## Idempotency

Running the analysis twice without changes between runs and without `--refresh-best-practices`
produces the same recommendations (deterministic ordering, no timestamps in recommendation
content). With `--refresh-best-practices`, recommendations may change because external
best-practice sources changed — this is expected, not a bug (DD-009-008).

## Authority boundary

- Never auto-apply changes without human approval.
- Never edit projection files directly — always via canonical sources + `acos --fix`.
- Never remove or rename entrypoints (that's `--reconcile`).
- Never create project-specific entrypoints (that's `1200-metaskill`).
- Preserve user customizations (`managed: false` rules, adopted rules, custom entrypoints,
  project-specific context sections).
- **Never propose a change without referencing the specific file, line, or pattern in the
  actual codebase that justifies it.** Generic recommendations without project-specific
  evidence are rejected.
